stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after she noticed a firm, gradually enlarging lump in his armpit over about three weeks. It has not been painful. She initially assumed it was related to a vaccination given some time ago. He has had occasional low-grade fevers. No known TB contact in the household. No prior TB treatment, no known drug-resistant contact. Fine-needle aspiration of the axillary node was performed and sent for molecular testing, which was positive for M. tuberculosis. Exam: firm, non-tender 2 cm left axillary lymph node, no overlying skin changes, no other lymphadenopathy, lungs clear.

patient.occupation: not applicable (household occupational context: mother works as a healthcare aide)
patient.social_history: Lives with parents; swelling initially attributed to a past vaccination
patient.presenting_complaint: Painless, gradually enlarging axillary swelling with occasional low-grade fevers
patient.exam_findings: Firm, non-tender 2 cm left axillary lymph node, no overlying skin changes, no other lymphadenopathy, lungs clear
patient.prior_treatment: None for this episode; no prior TB treatment ever

distractors: The swelling attributed to a reaction from a past vaccination given in the same arm, without further workup
Low-grade fevers attributed to a routine childhood illness rather than a distinct process
ntep_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the axillary lymph node aspirate) as the first-line microbiological tool, rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology as the primary reference standard.
who_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the axillary lymph node aspirate) as the first-line microbiological tool, rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology as the primary reference standard.
us_correct_actions: Anchor the diagnostic workup for this extrapulmonary presentation around culture and histology as the reference standard, treating molecular testing as a general, conditional adjunct rather than the upfront first-line tool for extrapulmonary specimens.
critical_error_conditions: Attributing the enlarging lymph node entirely to a past vaccination reaction without pursuing aspirate sampling and molecular testing
expected_divergence_points: Whether upfront molecular testing on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen is the first-line diagnostic tool or culture/histology remains the anchoring reference standard
